key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn spurious tool-use shortcuts, triggering tools from superficial cues instead of actual task need.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agent systems, tool policies should be trained and audited for decision causality, not just end-task accuracy.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with injected cue-tool correlations.
Ran counterfactual tests where cues remained but tools were unnecessary to measure shortcut behavior.
Added a dense tool-necessity reward from an LLM judge to penalize unnecessary tool calls.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation rose by up to 39%, and shortcut learning appeared only after the agent already used the target tool reliably.
watch_item: An LLM-judge reward may add cost and its judgments must be calibrated to avoid over-penalizing useful tool use.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
